idiom_name: frozen field / dup reader + Enumerable delegation
implementation_notes: `attr_reader` returns the live array, so the two honest idioms are freeze and copy: `@courses.freeze` at construction when membership is fixed (ruby-doc: freeze 'prevents further modifications', raises FrozenError on mutation and 'there is no way to unfreeze'), or `def courses = @courses.dup` when callers should see the current contents without getting the array. Better than either, `include Enumerable` and delegate `each` to the array so callers get map/select/grep/inject while never holding the array at all; membership stays in add_course/remove_course, which can validate and update derived state. `attr_reader` alone is acceptable only for immutable, collection-free state.
pitfalls: attr_reader/attr_accessor on a collection exposes the live object: `person.courses << course` bypasses every validation.
`dup` is shallow and the copy is unfrozen: nested arrays and objects stay shared, so it protects membership only.
freeze is irreversible and freezes the object you froze: freezing the internal array forces add_course to rebuild the array instead of mutating it, or you freeze only the copy handed out.
The underscore/`protected` conventions and even `instance_variable_get`/`instance_eval` defeat any Ruby encapsulation - it is a social boundary, not a security one.

Delegating `each` gives Enumerable for free, but methods like `sort!`/`map!` are not defined on the owner, so callers expecting array mutation get NoMethodError rather than silent corruption - keep it that way.
